Header:
Date: 2026-03-15
Start: 14:00 PDT
Duration: ~52 minutes
Recording id: ff-20260315-atlasml-01
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Natarajan (Redwood SE), Samira Khan (Atlas ML CTO), Evan Park (Atlas Head of ML Infra), Marcus Li (Atlas SRE)

Summary (auto): Technical deep dive on prefix/prompt caching strategy. Discussed cache key design, hit rates, eviction, multi-tenant isolation, security for VPC/on-prem, batching interactions, and quantization implications. Agreed next steps: share design doc, run benchmarks, schedule pilot kickoff.

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan: alright everyone, thanks for joining, uh this is Jordan from Redwood, i have Priya our SE with me, we'll do a deep dive on prefix caching, hit rates, multi-tenant concerns. was that okay for timing?
[00:18] Samira: yes perfect, we've been trying to understand trade offs - our main things are latency SLOs under 150ms and, and cloud egress limits because of regulations.
[00:29] Priya: awesome. quick agenda, we will run through how our runtime implements KV/prefix caching, what a cache key is, common strategies (prompt fingerprinting, conversation id, user-scoped keys), eviction policies, safety for multi-tenant, then latency/throughput numbers and how batching interacts. we'll leave time for questions.
[00:48] Evan: quick context - Atlas ML runs multi-tenant workloads, a mixture of chat and single-turn completion. A lot of prefixes are shared across users (templates, system prompts). we want to maximize hit rate without mixing PII between tenants.
[01:05] Priya: right. so starting from the top - the cache in Redwood is a prefix KV store of hidden states (KV cache) keyed by "cache key". we typically compute a fingerprint over the prefix tokens and configuration (model name, tokenizer version, temperature flags that change decoding state). common mistakes are omitting model variant or tokenizer which leads to silent corruption of hits.
[01:30] Marcus: when you say fingerprint, is that deterministic on-device or centralized? we worry about leaking across tenants if a hash collides.
[01:38] Priya: good question. we use SHA-256 over a canonicalized prefix blob + model id + quantization profile id. collision risk is effectively negligible. the keys are namespaced by customer id in Dedicated or Private - so multi-tenant safety is enforced at namespace level for hosted mode. for Private/VPC we recommend enforcing separate namespaces per tenant and optionally separate cache volumes.
[02:02] Samira: ok, we are private deployment on-prem so separate namespaces works. what about shared models that multiple tenants use - do you dedupe at model level?
[02:12] Priya: we can dedupe within the same namespace. cross-tenant dedupe is off by default for security reasons. if you want cross-tenant dedupe we can support it with encryption-wrapped keys and explicit contracts, but most enterprise customers prefer per-tenant isolation.
[02:28] Jordan: tradeoff: dedupe increases hit-rate and lowers cost but requires trust model + contractual handling of data.
[02:35] Evan: can you explain how batching affects prefix cache hits? our throughput is high and we rely on batching for throughput.
[02:42] Priya: yes. batching operates at runtime; prefixes are applied before the generation phase. if multiple requests in a batch share the same prefix key, we fetch once and broadcast the KV states into the batch. that gives near-linear savings. batching doesn't change the correctness of the cache; it changes latency profiles - large batches increase P95. Redwood has adaptive batching to cap latency and maintain SLOs.
[03:05] Marcus: we heard about adaptive batching but are concerned about tail latency. what's the knob to cap that?
[03:11] Priya: two knobs: max batch size and max wait time (ms). we typically recommend conservative max wait time for chat SLOs (e.g., 20ms) and larger for background bulk inference. there's also priority queuing so low-priority traffic can be batched more.
[03:26] Samira: about cache hit rates — what realistic numbers do you see? we have lots of templated system prompts, maybe 60% repeated prefixes.
[03:33] Priya: in similar customers we see prefix hit rates 40-80% depending on how templated the workload is. with dedupe + template normalization you'd be on the higher side. we have a sample benchmark (shared link) where templated chat reached 72% hit-rate and reduced token cost by ~38%.
[03:52] Evan: sounds good. what about eviction — lru? TTL? size-based? we need deterministic TTLs for compliance.
[03:59] Priya: we support layered policies: LRU by default, optional TTL, and size-based quotas per namespace. for regulated customers you can set strict TTLs and also enable audit logs for cache accesses. we also surface a cold/warm metric so you can see how often prefixes are re-populated.
[04:18] Marcus: do you persist caches to disk across restarts? in our on-prem clusters we want warm restarts.
[04:24] Priya: yes, persistent cache option: checkpoint to encrypted storage with configurable snapshot interval. for on-prem we integrate with customer KMS to encrypt snapshots. restore is best-effort; we also include versioning so incompatible caches don't get loaded.
[04:39] Samira: security — what about PII leaking because a cached prefix contained user-specific info?
[04:45] Priya: two mitigations: first, canonicalization / normalization to strip PII from prefixes before fingerprinting (recommended), second, namespace isolation. third, content tagging — you can mark prefixes as non-cacheable if they include sensitive flags. we also provide tooling to scan cache entries for high-entropy strings.
[05:05] Evan: how do you detect differences caused by quantization? e.g., 4-bit vs 8-bit models produce different hidden states right?
[05:12] Priya: exactly. cache keys include quantization profile id and kernel set id. we don't share caches across incompatible quantization configs. if you upgrade quantization, the cache will miss until re-populated. we recommend running a small rollback-aware rollout when changing quantization to avoid regressions.
[05:29] Jordan: Priya, can you show the short example config?
[05:32] Priya: sure i will paste in chat but briefly: you declare namespace: atlas-prod, key_scheme: sha256(prefix_tokens + model_id + tokenizer_version + q_profile), ttl: 24h, eviction: lru, persistent: true, encrypt_snapshots: true.
[05:49] Samira: nice. what about metrics — do you expose per-key hit/miss counters and latency breakdowns?
[05:55] Priya: per-namespace hit/miss rates, per-model metrics, and token-level savings. also traces per request with cache events so you can see when a miss causes extra generation. these are available in Redwood Console and via our metrics endpoint.
[06:10] Evan: for our pilot, we want a synthetic bench: 50k req/day, 60% templated, measure hit rate, token savings, and p95 latency. Jordan, is that doable?
[06:18] Jordan: yes we'll provide benchmark harness and sample workload; Priya will provide config.
[06:22] Marcus: one last concern — multi-tenant side channels, timing attacks to infer presence of a prefix. is that a vector?
[06:29] Priya: agreed it's possible. mitigations: per-tenant namespaces, constant-time response padding, and don't expose raw cache hit metrics cross-tenant. for hosted customers we disable cross-tenant dedupe and avoid exposing hit-level APIs except to the owning tenant.
[06:45] Samira: great. any gotchas around function-calling or tool-calls and caching? we do tool-augmented prompts.
[06:52] Priya: tool calls usually change the state machine; we key by the prefix including tool spec. if tool results are dynamic, mark those prefixes non-cacheable or use short TTLs.
[07:06] Jordan: ok we'll recap after a couple more Qs.
[07:10] Samira: about VPC/on-prem deployment: does Redwood support sidecar cache vs centralized cache? we prefer sidecar for lower blast radius.
[07:18] Priya: yes sidecar per node is supported; we also offer centralized sharded cache within a private VPC. sidecar gives local low-latency reads but has lower cross-request dedupe. centralized offers higher dedupe but some network hop. both support TLS + mTLS and KMS encryption.
[07:36] Evan: do you have rough numbers for added hop latency for central cache?
[07:40] Priya: on a colocated VPC it's ~1-3ms median, 5-12ms p95 depending on network. sidecar is <1ms median. tradeoff again between hit-rate gains and extra latency.
[07:53] Marcus: our compliance team will want audit logs for cache access - is that present?
[07:58] Priya: yes audit logs, include key fingerprints, namespace, timestamp, event type (read/write/evict). logs can be shipped to your SIEM, with obfuscation options.
[08:10] Samira: thanks this answered most of our questions. next steps?
[08:14] Jordan: we'll share the design doc and config, provide benchmark harness. Evan will run the bench. we'll reconvene after Evan's bench results. scheduling now?
[08:23] Evan: send 2 windows next week for pilot kickoff.
[08:26] Jordan: noted. thanks everyone.
